statement_text: The corrective maintenance request process is clearly defined and effective.
Corrective maintenance response times are tracked and reviewed for trends.
Service response expectations for clinical staff are formally defined and communicated.
The current CMMS coding structure for work order request, result, and fault support needed corrective maintenance reporting.
Corrective maintenance turnaround times are tracked and analyzed effectively.
Equipment risk classification, including life support, high-risk, and critical designations, is determined using a defined and consistently applied methodology.
3.	Device eligibility for an AEM program is determined using defined data elements and risk-scoring criteria.
Responsibility for performing risk classification on new devices entering the hospital is clearly assigned.
Assets included in an AEM program are clearly identified within the asset management system.
The department has an effective mechanism to monitor whether failure rates change after devices are placed in an AEM program.
Preventive maintenance workload is distributed evenly across available staff or work groups.
The department maintains the MEMP in a current state.
The department effectively follows the requirements of the MEMP.
Employees demonstrate understanding of their individual responsibilities for MEMP compliance.
Recalls and hazard alerts are managed through a closed-loop process that verifies completion and resolution.
The department is effectively notified when any new equipment (purchased, loaner, rental, demo, and patient-owned) is scheduled to enter the facility.

statement_text: Documented labor is accurately captured and reviewed for trends across modality, technicians, and facilities.
Preventive maintenance and corrective maintenance labor times are benchmarked against industry standards or relevant external comparators.
Critical equipment downtime reports are reviewed and used to evaluate service performance.
Employee goals are reviewed periodically throughout the year.
Employees clearly understand their daily and weekly performance responsibilities.
Employees are able to communicate with supervisors about operational observations and improvement opportunities.
The department has an effective orientation and onboarding process.
The department has a career ladder that appropriately supports staff development.
The department has a defined succession planning process.
Employees understand how their roles contribute to the department’s mission, vision, and goals.
Ancillary costs, such as training, test equipment, implementation needs, and related expenses, are incorporated into replacement planning.
Equipment replacement decisions are made using defined criteria and a consistent decision-making process.
HTM plays a significant role in the organizations capital replacement planning process.
Customer satisfaction surveys that assess all aspects of HTM service delivery are conducted on a regular basis
Customer satisfaction survey results are reviewed with an eye on continuous process improvement.
Poor customer satisfaction survey results translate into comprehensive action plans for remediation.
Department policies are well-documented and readily available.
Department policies are reviewed and updated on a regular annual schedule.
Employees consistently review and reaffirm applicable policies each year.
Policy compliance is consistently monitored and enforced.
Cost of service ratio is accurately determined and monitored.
Cost of service ratio is analyzed by hospital, technician, device type, and comparable departments as applicable.
The methodology for determining cost of service ratio is clearly defined and consistently applied.
Ratios that fall outside of established norms are analyzed for root cause and remediation.
Preventive maintenance completion benchmarks are established and monitored.
Corrective maintenance completion benchmarks are established and monitored.
The department has a clearly defined and effective communication policy for Staff, Customer, and Executive Leadership updates.
Safety rounds are used effectively to proactively identify nonconforming equipment.
Safety rounds are a closed-loop process that assign nonconformance items for remediation and feedback to the appropriate committee.
Inventory validation activities are performed periodically throughout the year.
Device nomenclature, including manufacturer, model, and device category, is clean, standardized, and consistently applied.
The department has a current and clearly defined asset disposition process that includes transfers, sales, trade-ins, donations, and disposals.
Assets are defined and prioritized for disposition using consistent criteria.
Final asset dispositions are accurately tracked and recorded.
The annual monetary value of all assets dispositions is tracked and reviewed.
The parts ordering process is clearly defined and effectively addresses centralized and decentralized purchasing responsibilities.
Parts usage and costs are accurately tracked and reviewed.
Parts needs for preventive maintenance work are forecasted using a defined process.
Equipment downtime attributable to waiting for parts is tracked and analyzed.
Ancillary parts costs, including rush shipping and related expenses, are tracked and reviewed.
Part requests are aggregated by vendor.
Parts quality relative to DOAs, late part deliveries, wrong part deliveries, and premature failures are assessed on an ongoing basis.
User-related error trends are tracked and analyzed by model, department, or other relevant category.
User-related error trends are escalated to nursing, nursing education, or other appropriate stakeholders through a defined notification process.
The department participates appropriately in Risk Management’s annual FMEA process.
Equipment, including disposables, involved in a patient incident follows a defined and effective process for investigation and root cause analysis.
The process for purchasing new and renewing existing service contracts is clearly defined and effective.
HTM is appropriately represented in service contract decision-making.
Service contract information is accurately maintained and identifiable in the current CMMS.
Service vendors are evaluated to ensure they meet applicable regulatory requirements.
Vendor service performance is reviewed to determine overall satisfaction and effectiveness.
Completed vendor service activities are received, documented, and tracked consistently.
Contract value analysis processes effectively support decisions about contracted versus in-house service.
HTM is appropriately involved in any and all technology management opportunities in your organization.
